saving-unit: % shaft power reduction for a 2% impeller diameter reduction
note: 'a 2% reduction in the impeller diameter creates about a 2% reduction in flow, a 4% reduction in head, and an 8% reduction in power' (affinity-law approximation for small changes). Energy savings roughly proportional to the cube of the diameter reduction; impellers rarely trimmed below 70% of original diameter.

measure: Select a higher-efficiency centrifugal pump (81% vs 78% at operating point)
note: Worked example: 15,000 gpm, 150 ft head, 700-hp motor, 8,000 h/yr, motor 96%; 27 bhp reduction; $8,393/yr at 5 cents/kWh; 15-year pump life gives $125,888 lifetime savings. COST BASIS: incremental. PRICE YEAR NOT STATED; example uses 5 cents/kWh; tip sheet dated October 2005, sourcebook 2006.

measure: Restore a degraded pump to its design efficiency (55% to 78%)
note: Worked example: 300-hp centrifugal pump drawing 235 kW, 6,000 h/yr; $20,786/yr at 5 cents/kWh. Savings = kWin x t x (1 - eta_a/eta_o). Repair cost not given. PRICE YEAR NOT STATED; example uses 5 cents/kWh; tip sheet dated October 2005, sourcebook 2006.

measure: Maintenance of wear rings and rotor (prevent erosion losses)
saving-unit: % wire-to-water efficiency loss avoided (printed as 10% or more)
note: 'Wear ring and rotor erosions ... can reduce the wire-to-water efficiency of pumps by 10% or more.' A pump's efficiency can degrade as much as 10-25% before it is replaced (p.109).

measure: Right-size an oversized pump (add a 50-bhp pump for 9 months of the year in place of a 200-hp pump)
note: Worked example: chilled water, 3,500 gpm pump replaced most of the year by a 1,250 gpm pump at the same head; motors 93%; $39,525/yr at 5 cents/kWh. New-pump cost not given. PRICE YEAR NOT STATED; example uses 5 cents/kWh; tip sheet dated October 2005, sourcebook 2006.

saving-unit: % reduction in friction factor (printed as more than 40%)
note: Friction factor can be reduced 'by more than 40%, proportionately reducing your pumping costs' (frictional component only). Pipe-size example (600 gpm, 10,000 ft, 70% pump+motor efficiency): annual friction pumping cost $16,900 (6-inch), $4,250 (8-inch), $1,400 (10-inch) at 5 cents/kWh (p.115).

measure: High-efficiency motor in place of a standard motor at replacement
payback: attractive payback in high-use applications (no number)
note: 'High-efficiency motors are generally 3% to 8% more efficient than standard ones.' Also in the fan sourcebook p.27 (doe_2003_002).
Generic statement for DOE plant assessments; energy costs can be 10% or more of plant operating costs.
